For chaotic systems, however, individual trajectories become unpredictable beyond a finite predictability horizon, and plausible states need not form plausible trajectories. Beyond this horizon, the objective should shift from predicting a particular future to generating trajectories that preserve both the statistics of physical states and their temporal evolution. We study this as an objective-design problem using a Jump-and-Complete framework that factorizes trajectory generation into two stochastic tasks: a Jumper samples plausible distant endpoints, and a Completer generates the paths connecting the observed context to those endpoints. Both are trained with the Energy Score and evaluated with state- and path-space diagnostics. On 2D Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Kolmogorov flow, we first show that, past the predictability horizon, pointwise errors fail to distinguish models with very different temporal behavior. We then show that two seemingly auxiliary design choices shape the learned trajectory distribution. First, training the Completer on Jumper-sampled rather than exact endpoints changes which temporal statistics of composed rollouts are matched on Kolmogorov flow. Second, sharing one latent draw across a trajectory preserves temporal dependence better than resampling noise at each time, despite an equal or better Energy Score. Thus, for stochastic trajectory learning, the effective objective is determined not only by the loss, but also by what the model is conditioned on during training and how randomness is shared across time.

title: SO(3)-RoPE for Spherical Transformers
abstract:
Many scientific domains produce data that lives on the sphere.
Most spherical transformer architectures violate the spherical geometry,
introducing distortions and coordinate singularities at the poles.
We develop a RoPE-like position embedding, depending only on relative spherical locations.
They act via unitary SO3 representations and lead to SO3-equivariant attention.
Our SO3-RoPE is compatible with FlashAttention and thus retains the throughput and memory efficiency of vanilla transformers.
We evaluate our method on a shallow water dynamics prediction task on a rotating sphere.
It outperforms an S2Transformer baseline while having lower wall-clock time.

title: Distilling Dark Matter Halo Profiles: Symbolic Regression on Rotation Curve Data
abstract:
Rotation curves of spiral galaxies directly probe the underlying dark matter halo structure, yet no halo profile model universally describes the diversity observed across galaxies. We use symbolic regression applied to the Spitzer Photometry \& Accurate
Rotation Curves (SPARC) database to distil a new family of dark matter halo velocity profiles directly from observational data. The resulting expression is parameterised by an amplitude $c$, dimensionless radial coordinate $x$, and a galaxy-specific shape parameter $\gamma$.
To formally evaluate performance, we fit the new profile, alongside seven established literature profiles, to SPARC using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. Trained on a subset of 115 galaxies from the 175-galaxy sample, the profile achieves good fits, as defined by a reduced chi-squared statistic $\chi^2_\nu<2$, on 81\% of the out-of-distribution test sample and 76\% of the full SPARC sample, outperforming all comparison profiles. We interpret the model physically, and quantify the correlation between the model parameters and observable galaxy properties, thereby exploring the link between dark matter halo structure and galaxy morphology. The results demonstrate the potential of symbolic regression as a tool for data-driven discovery in galactic dynamics.

title: Which Physical Symmetries Can Be Imposed by Averaging?
abstract: Averaging a trained model over a compact symmetry group makes it invariant, and when the data share the symmetry the averaged model is no worse than the original under a convex loss. Many symmetries of physical systems, such as translations, Lorentz boosts and changes of units, form non-compact groups, so the average must be restricted to a bounded set of group elements, usually a ball around the identity. We study what this truncation preserves. For connected Lie groups, ball averages become invariant for every bounded model if and only if the volume of balls grows polynomially. Under exponential growth, as for the Lorentz group, they do not, and the average is governed by the values of the model at the cutoff. In addition, no data distribution is invariant under a non-compact group that moves inputs arbitrarily far, as translations and boosts do. The guarantee that averaging does not increase the risk is then lost, as an exact counterexample and a trained top-quark tagger show. Amenability decides neither question. It decides only whether some other sequence of sets makes the average invariant, and we construct such sets for the affine and similarity groups.

title: A Catalog-Free Spatio-Spectral Representation of the Sky
abstract: Astronomical surveys observe the same sky through instruments with different bandpasses, point-spread functions, apertures, and noise properties, and standard coaddition offers no way to combine a fiber spectrum with a broadband image. We model the sky as a single continuous spectral surface-brightness field, fit directly to calibrated single-epoch measurements, each modeled as an integral of the field against its instrument's own measurement kernel (astrometry, PSF or line-spread function, bandpass or wavelength bin, and aperture). An implementation with $9.2\times10^6$ anisotropic Gaussian components and 32 shared nonnegative spectral templates jointly fits 405 SDSS exposures and 889 SDSS/BOSS fiber spectra over an $84'\times84'$ COSMOS field without an external source catalog. The in-sample forward model recovers integrated source flux in these fibers, with the known sky subtracted, to 5.5\% median absolute fractional error. We then omit complete exposures from optimization, initialization, and component lifecycle, retain other bands and spectra as same-sky conditioning, and synthesize the omitted frames through their recorded operators. In four holdouts with more than 70\% of the footprint lacking same-band coverage, hole-region flux ratios range from 0.71 to 1.86, versus 0.90--1.06 for matched in-sample controls. Coverage stratification separates supported from unsupported synthesis and localizes the failures. The result is both a scalable shared representation and a falsifiable protocol for testing observation-operator transfer.

title: GyroSplat: A Linear Representation of Fusion Plasma Turbulence with Direct and Differentiable Physics
abstract: Gyrokinetic simulations model the plasma turbulence governing heat transport in magnetically confined fusion devices. These 5D simulations are computationally expensive and produce massive data volumes, with a single snapshot requiring tens of gigabytes of storage. This makes directly storing intermediate timesteps impractical and motivates the use of (lossy) compression. Recent neural compression approaches achieve favorable rate–distortion trade-offs by augmenting conventional $L_2$ reconstruction objectives with physics-informed losses that preserve derived quantities such as the electrostatic potential and heat flux. However, neural network based representations can be difficult to optimize and refine when additional constraints are imposed. We introduce GyroSplat, a compression method for gyrokinetic fields inspired by Gaussian splatting. GyroSplat represents each plasma field as a weighted sum of independent Gaussian–Gabor atoms, yielding a representation that is linear in its coefficients. This linearity enables a staged optimization strategy in which atoms are first fitted to minimize reconstruction error, then refined against the potential, and subsequently new atoms are added to correct the transport. Moreover, relevant derived quantities admit closed-form expressions in terms of the atom coefficients, enabling efficient refinement via a Gauss–Newton procedure. Experiments on gyrokinetic simulation data show that GyroSplat achieves improved trade-offs at matched storage over established compression baselines on derived physical quantities while remaining competitive on field reconstruction, and improving over state-of-the-art physics-informed compressors. These results demonstrate Gaussian splatting as an effective and flexible approach to high-fidelity compression of scientific simulation data.

title: Anatomy of Rollout Error in Chaotic Flow Surrogates
abstract:
Autoregressive neural surrogates for turbulent PDEs are typically evaluated by
rollout RMSE against a reference trajectory. However, in chaotic flows, trajectories
often decorrelate due to sensitivity to initial conditions, making pointwise predic-
tion errors meaningless. We investigate how surrogate errors develop and what
aspects of the learned dynamics can still be evaluated beyond this predictability
horizon. We compare deterministic and generative surrogates on 2D Kolmogorov
flow using a shared backbone, focusing on models whose rollouts remain bounded.
Our analysis reveals three findings. First, errors emerge at fine spatial scales before
large-scale trajectory decorrelation. Second, despite trajectory divergence, local
one-step errors measured against a numerical solver on model-generated states
remain approximately constant with rollout depth. Third, one-step prediction ac-
curacy does not necessarily translate into accurate long-term state statistics. This
highlights the need to complement trajectory-based evaluation with measures of
local dynamical accuracy and long-term statistical fidelity.

title: Task-Agnostic Self-Supervised Learning for Physical Dynamics
abstract:
Physics foundation models are commonly pretrained by forecasting future states, tying representation learning to a specific downstream task. We investigate whether self-supervised learning from partial observations can instead produce task-agnostic representations that capture the hidden dynamics of physical systems. Using a shared ViT backbone for heterogeneous 2D and 3D systems, we study masked reconstruction in physical space and JEPA-style prediction in latent space. To assess what these representations encode about the underlying dynamics, we freeze the encoder and measure how well governing physical parameters can be recovered from its features.
To explicitly target properties of the dynamical system that persist across an entire trajectory, we introduce \emph{regime fingerprinting}, which exploits the fact that an early partial view and a broader view of the same trajectory are generated under the same physical regime, and trains their representations to remain identifiable across time. Combined with latent-space prediction, regime fingerprinting yields the strongest recovery of governing parameters in our experiments and compares favorably with forecasting-pretrained baselines. These results suggest that self-supervised learning can capture trajectory-level physical dynamics without using forecasting as a pretraining objective.

title: Grid, Set, or Graph? Representations for Learned VLBI Reconstruction Under Distribution Shift
abstract: Radio interferometers measure complex visibilities at irregularly sampled spatial frequencies, with sampling patterns that vary between observations. We investigate how the representation of these measurements affects learned image reconstruction by comparing three approaches: a regular grid processed by a convolutional neural network (CNN), an unordered set processed by DeepSets, and a $k$-nearest-neighbour graph processed by a graph neural network (GNN). The models are trained to reproduce CLEAN images from Astrogeo X-band observations and evaluated without adaptation on the MOJAVE 15 GHz survey. The GNN achieves the lowest median normalized mean squared error (NMSE) on both held-out X-band observations (0.202, compared with 0.228 for DeepSets and 0.376 for the CNN) and MOJAVE (0.386, compared with 0.448 and 0.707). However, all three models exhibit similar relative increases in NMSE under the survey shift (88–96\%), providing no clear evidence of differences in relative robustness. An oracle-scaled mean-image baseline outperforms all three models, while diagnostics on selected observations suggest that amplitude underprediction contributes substantially to the degradation on MOJAVE. Because the survey shift simultaneously changes observing frequency, array configuration, and source characteristics, these results do not isolate the effects of sampling geometry.
